power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > 0.10", "p<0.005", "p-value > 0.01", 
"p < 0.05", "p < 0.05", "p < 0.05"), Text = c("Overall, for top CpGs, there was low correlation in the effect estimates across sex-analyses (r ranged from 0.03 to 0.08, p > 0.10).", 
"Compared to other CpGs analyzed across the genome, the top CpGs associated with ePTB in the boys' and girls' analyses were more likely to be found in open sea regions than expected by chance (p<0.005; Supplementary Fig 1), rather than within CpG islands, or any other genomic region.", 
"Probes with detection p-value > 0.01 (n=1,937) and bead number lower than three (n=90) in more than 20% of the samples were excluded.", 
"First, to account for the correlation between CpGs across the genome, and to more comprehensively examine associations, we looked at genomic regions rather than individual CpGs by conducting a differentially methylated regional (DMR) analysis using dmrff R package. 60 We selected robustly associated DMRs at regional Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.05 and CpG count above one.", 
"DMRs were selected at regional Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.05.", 
"DHS: CpGs identified across analyses were primarily enriched in Open Sea regions (p < 0.05)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > 0.10", "p-value > 0.01 "), Sentence = c("Overall, for top CpGs, there was low correlation in the effect estimates across sex-analyses (r ranged from 0.03 to 0.08, p > 0.10).", "Probes with detection p-value > 0.01 (n=1,937) and bead number lower than three (n=90) in more than 20% of the samples were excluded." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Preterm birth (PTB) affects 11% of pregnancies worldwide, yet the biological mechanisms underlying its etiology remain unclear.
We conducted a sex-stratified epigenome-wide association study of newborn saliva DNA methylation in 273 mother-child pairs from the Peruvian Placental Abruption Genetic Epidemiology (PAGE) study.

Robust linear regression models adjusted for maternal, cellular, and technical factors identified 318 and 542 ePTBassociated CpG sites and 784 and 1,401 differentially methylated regions in boys and girls, respectively, with limited overlap between sexes.

Functional analyses revealed enrichment of signals in Open Sea regions and pathways related to neurodevelopment, neural function, fetal growth, cellular organization, transcription factors, and microRNAs.
Several associations replicated findings from prior studies of PTB, gestational age, and postmenstrual age.
These results identify sex-specific epigenetic signatures of ePTB in an Admixed-American population and highlight developmental and regulatory pathways associated with ePTB.
Preterm birth (PTB) is a leading cause of neonatal and infant morbidity and mortality.

PTB is associated with long-term health impairments for the newborn, including respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage, neurodevelopmental delays and mortality in adulthood. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] PTB affects around 11% of pregnancies worldwide, totaling nearly 15 million births. 6 Despite its substantial public health impact, the biological mechanisms underlying PTB and early PTB (ePTB), a more extreme outcome representing births occurring 34 weeks of gestation, remain insufficiently understood.

text.text: Epigenetic processes, particularly DNA methylation (DNAm), are increasingly recognized as central in fetal development and may provide insight into biological pathways associated with PTB and its subsequent health consequences.

Maternal psychosocial stressors, including history of trauma exposure and mood disorders, are known risk factors for PTB and adverse neonatal outcomes. 1, [7] [8] [9] These exposures have been linked to DNAm variation in pathways related to stress regulation, immune function, and neurodevelopment, suggesting a plausible biological route through which maternal experiences shape offspring health. text.text: Our study analyzed data from 273 mother-child dyads, of which 139 were cases of ePTB.
Sex-stratified analyses identified 318 and 542 CpG sites with saliva methylation levels associated with ePTB in boys and girls, respectively.

Most of these sites were hypomethylated, which is consistent with the literature, as increasing gestational age is associated with more hypermethylated sites. 25 Only 24 of these sites overlapped between sexes, indicating substantial sex heterogeneity in the observed associations.

text.text: In secondary analyses, we identified 784 and 1,401 DMRs associated with ePTB for boys and girls, respectively.

Enrichment analyses revealed further distinctions: boys exhibited enrichment of ePTB-associated pathways across well-defined biological processes, with a focus on neurodevelopment, whereas girls predominantly showed enrichment for regulatory pathways, with transcription factors and micro-RNAs being the most common pathways identified.
We discuss the results separately for each sex.
Forty-five percent of the CpG sites significantly associated with ePTB in boys were hypermethylated.
The most significant hypermethylated CpG site by p-value is a novel site for ePTB mapping to a long non-coding RNA region near SLFNL1 Antisense RNA 1 (SLFNL1-AS1).

Experimental evidence has shown that SLFNL1-AS1 interacts with proteins encoded by HNRNPH1, a gene that plays a critical role in cancer development. 30 The two most significant hypomethylated sites were also previously unreported CpG sites, both mapping to an intergenic region near the Dopamine Receptor D1 (DRD1), which encodes the most abundant dopamine receptor in the brain and has been implicated in mental and neuronal diseases 31 .

text.text: Lastly, a pathway related to insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) and Akt signaling was found with enrichment among ePTB-associated CpGs in boys.

This pathway is important because proteins in the IGF-axis are associated with cellular growth, proliferation, and metabolism throughout the life course, and IGF1 is particularly related with fetal growth and development 37 , and with postnatal growth. 38 These findings suggest that DNAm differences associated with ePTB may involve pathways relevant to fetal and postnatal growth.

text.text: Lastly, we identified a KCNQ2 and KCNQ3-related epilepsy pathway.

KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 are part of a family of voltage-gated potassium channel proteins with a function in cellular excitatory activity, particularly in the brain. 44 Pathogenic variants in these genes have been associated with neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (NEO-DEE), self-limited (benign) familial neonatal epilepsy (SLFNE), and with neurodevelopmental disorder with or without seizures (NDD) 45 .

text.text: Our study provides novel CpG sites, DMRs, and pathways associated with ePTB in an Admixed-American population.

Additionally, several signals overlapped with findings from studies conducted predominantly in populations of European ancestry, suggesting that some ePTB-associated DNAm patterns may be shared across population groups.
To ensure our results were robust, we controlled for cell composition and batch effects and used Bacon adjustment to reduce genomic inflation.
We also thoroughly inspected for data structure and reduced latent variation in DNAm by stratifying our data and analyses by sex.

To verify the reliability of our findings, we applied a negative control analysis, corrected for multiple testing using an epigenome-wide significance threshold recommended for the EPIC array, and compared our results with existing evidence.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first such study in a South American population, helping to reduce gaps in epigenetic research across populations.
Our study also has some limitations.
Due to the cross-sectional study design, we cannot make causal claims, as we cannot determine from these data when DNAm differences occurred, whether before or after delivery.

Even though timing of sample collection relative to delivery was known for these participants (within 72 hours), precise assessment of PMA and other markers of aging and development among preterms was not possible as we did not have information about time of discharge from the NICU.

In relation to the above, differences in DNAm observed could have been associated with other pregnancy complications related to ePTB, or with stressful exposures occurring at or around delivery rather than by ePTB alone; this possibility warrants further examination.

The methylation data were obtained from saliva, which may not reflect methylation in other tissues, like brain, blood, or placenta which are more often utilized for the study of fetal neurodevelopment.

We identified many novel associations that may be attributable to population differences 47 and/or to higher rates of maternal prenatal stressors that could influence the relationship between ePTB and dysregulation in newborn DNAm.

text.text: These possibilities require further study in similar populations.

Our study identified multiple novel epigenetic associations with ePTB in an admixed-Amerindian sample of Peruvian women, while also replicating some associations previously reported in European samples.
These results suggest that ePTB-associated DNAm patterns include both signals shared with previous population groups and signals that may be population-specific or phenotype-specific.
We also observed sex-specific associations with ePTB, with few signals shared between boys and girls.
In both cases, most differentially methylated sites were hypomethylated in relation to ePTB, which is consistent with the existing literature (hypermethylation with increasing GA or aging).

Although pathways enriched in differentially methylated genes for ePTB consistently pointed to neurodevelopment, cellular growth and function, immune response, and neurological outcomes, our results showed that for girls these processes were more influenced by regulatory elements like transcription factors and micro-RNAs, while for boys it was by the biological process or molecular function itself, suggesting sex-specific patterns in the epigenetic features associated with ePTB.

Replication in independent and diverse populations, ideally with longitudinal biospecimen collection, will be important for determining the timing, reproducibility, and potential biological relevance of these associations.
Mother-child pairs included in the study were part of the Placental Abruption Genetic Epidemiology (PAGE) study, a case-control study conducted in Lima, Peru.

Description of the study can be found elsewhere. 48, 49 Briefly, eligible women were recruited at delivery from seven hospitals in Lima, Peru, by reviewing admission logbooks for the emergency room, labor and delivery wards, prenatal wards, emergency, and surgery rooms of the study hospitals, between March 2013 and December 2015.

text.text: Eligibility criteria included speaking Spanish, being > 18 years old, having a singleton pregnancy, and complete medical information to define ePTB status.

text.text: All study participants gave their written informed consent; the study protocols were approved by the IRB of the seven participating hospitals in Lima, the Swedish Medical Center, Seattle, WA, and the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

Information on sociodemographic (age, employment, marital status), lifestyle (smoking and alcohol use in pregnancy), behavioral, and anthropometric variables (pre-pregnancy BMI), were gathered using structured questionnaires.

Obstetric history and medical information of the current pregnancy (gestational age at delivery, gravidity, planned pregnancy, mode of delivery, birthweight, sex, discharge status, and APGAR score) were abstracted from medical records.

Gestational age at delivery (weeks) was calculated using information from the date of the last menstrual period, and from an early fetal ultrasound and fundal height examinations performed < 20 weeks of gestation.

text.text: Early preterm birth was defined following the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology criteria as a delivery occurring 20-34 weeks of gestation. 50 Based on their pathophysiology, 51 cases are either grouped as spontaneous (45%) or with preterm premature rupture of fetal membranes (PPROM; 54%).

text.text: There were no cases of medically induced PTB.
Controls were women who delivered at term (> 37 weeks and < 42 weeks of gestation) and were randomly selected from the participating hospitals within 48 hours of the identification of a case.

text.text: For the current study, we randomly selected 152 mom-child dyads with ePTB and 152 matched controls from the entire cohort with complete covariates of interest, and archived newborn biosamples with the highest quality of genomic DNA extracted from saliva samples collected 72 hours post-delivery (total eligible N=1,009 , n=468 with ePTB).
Newborn buccal cells were collected post-delivery, plated, and stored using the Oragene™saliva cell collection kits (OGR250, DNA Genotek Ottawa, Canada).

Samples were processed at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center (Buffalo, NY) for DNA extraction using Qiagen DNeasy™ system (Qiagen, Valencia, CA), and DNA methylation quantification using llumina MethylationEPIC v2 Beadarray (Illumina, San Diego, CA).
For DNAm assessment, 500 ng of genomic DNA from each sample was plated at random into 96-well plates, followed by bisulphite conversion treatment using the Zymo EZ DNA methylation kit.
This was followed by amplification, fragmentation, hybridization, single-base extension, and staining.
Methylation levels were analyzed at 937,055 CpGs across the genome.

Before analyses, DNAm data were pre-processed using the meffil R package, 52 where probes were quantile normalized using the first twenty principal components (PC) from the control probe matrix, and samples excluded based on outliers for the median methylated or unmethylated signal (n=1), sex-mismatch between reported and predicted sex (n=15), and X-Y ratio outliers (n=5).

text.text: We identified that sex was driving a large proportion of the underlying variation in DNAm.
Thus, our main analysis was stratified by sex.
We selected covariates a priori based on supporting literature, and by inspection of variability and multicollinearity.

We included as covariates maternal age (missing n=2), gravidity (missing n=3), pre-pregnancy BMI (Kg/m 2 ) (missing n=5), and employment in pregnancy (missing n=1), as these are established confounders in prenatal epigenetic studies, and known risk factors for PTB. 28, 54, 55 In addition, we adjusted for batch effects and the proportion of epithelial cells and seven immune cell types predicted using DNAm data. 53 We did not include ethnicity (most participants were mixed Amerindian and European descent by genetic ancestry analysis) 48 and maternal smoking (< 3% smokers) as covariates, as they showed low variability in our sample.

To reduce remaining variance in the test statistic and the likelihood of false positives, estimates of the EWAS were further corrected using bacon adjustment. 58 To account for multiple testing, statistical significance was defined using a p-value threshold < 9.4x10 -8 , consistent with recommendations for the Illumina EPIC array. 59 "Top CpGs" were defined based on p-value and an absolute effect estimate > 0.1.

In a sensitivity analysis, we checked for systematic sources of bias in our data by conducting a negative control analysis.
In this analysis, we used the complete sample (N=273 dyads), permuted ePTB status, adjusted for the same covariates as in the main analysis, and tested for genome-wide associations.

Obtaining similar results between the negative control analysis and the main analysis would suggest the presence of residual confounding in the main analysis or other systematic sources of bias still present in the data.
